opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's definitely shifted. A few years ago, and I think this was true for a lot of people in the field, the prevailing belief was that scale was basically the whole game. You make the model bigger, you throw more data and compute at it, and capabilities just keep emerging. And to be fair, that worked remarkably well for a long time. The jump from the early transformer models to what we had a few years later was largely a scaling story.

But I think we've hit the point where pure scale is giving diminishing returns relative to the cost. You can still get gains, but spending ten times more compute for a model that's marginally better on benchmarks isn't a great trade, especially for enterprises that need to run these things affordably in production.

So where I've landed is that scale is necessary but not sufficient. A lot of the progress now comes from other places: better data, especially synthetic data and data that teaches reasoning rather than just memorizing the internet; post-training and reinforcement learning; giving models time to think at inference instead of answering in one shot; and tool use, letting the model take actions, search, call APIs, and check its own work. Those things aren't free, but they're often a much more efficient path to capability than just making the base model bigger.

There's also a gap that scale alone doesn't close: models still struggle to learn continuously from experience the way people do. You deploy a model and it's frozen. It doesn't get better at your company's specific workflows by doing them. Solving that, whether through memory, online learning, or something else, will take real research, not just a bigger cluster.

So I'm still very optimistic about where the technology is going. I just don't think the path from here is "add more GPUs." It's a mix of engineering, data, and some genuinely new ideas.

r001.rationale: The speaker says his view has shifted from the field’s belief that scale was “basically the whole game,” citing strong gains from scaling. In context, this communicates his earlier provisional belief that scaling could provide the needed capabilities.

r002.rationale: He states that “scale is necessary but not sufficient” and describes other approaches needed for further capability gains.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it's changed quite a bit. When I was at Google working on the Transformer, and even in the early days of Cohere, I think a lot of us had this view that scale was the whole story. You throw more data and more compute at these models and they just keep getting better, and eventually you arrive at something that can do everything. And to be fair, that was borne out for a long time. Each generation of model, we scaled up and we saw these big step changes in capability.

But I've become a lot more skeptical that scale alone gets us all the way there. A few things pushed me in that direction. One is that we started hitting a data wall. There's only so much high-quality human-written text on the internet, and we've basically consumed it. So the "just add more data" lever has gotten much harder to pull. The second is that pre-training scaling started showing diminishing returns. You go from ten billion to a hundred billion parameters and the gains are enormous. You go from a hundred billion to a trillion and the gains are real but much smaller, and the cost is ten times higher. That's not a sustainable curve.

What I think actually matters now is what we do beyond pre-training. Reinforcement learning, synthetic data, test-time compute, letting the model reason for longer, use tools, interact with its environment. Those have delivered a lot of the recent progress, and they're not really "scaling" in the classic sense. They're new methods. So my view today is that scale is necessary but not sufficient. You still need big models, but the frontier is going to be defined by the algorithms and the data pipelines we layer on top, not just by how many GPUs you can buy.

And from Cohere's perspective, that's actually good news. If the only thing that mattered was raw compute, the biggest labs would win by default. The fact that there's real innovation left to do means the game is still open.

r001.rationale: He says he once thought more data and compute would eventually produce a model that could do everything, based on large capability gains across model generations.

r002.rationale: He says he is now skeptical that scale alone is enough and summarizes his view as “necessary but not sufficient.”

astra-6.text:
I’ve become less convinced that scaling alone gets us everything we need. I still think it’s incredibly powerful, and I expect bigger models to keep getting better. But that’s different from saying we can take the current recipe, put more compute into it, and get every capability we’re looking for.

Reasoning is a good example. You want a model to be able to spend more time on a difficult problem, check its work, and revise an approach that isn’t working. That’s a different dimension from just making the model larger during training. And if you want it to learn from interacting with the world, you need more than a fixed collection of text.

So I wouldn’t frame it as scaling versus new ideas. Scaling makes new ideas work better, and new ideas give us more useful things to scale. I’m still optimistic about the progress ahead; I’m less attached to the idea that there’s one recipe that takes us all the way.

r001.rationale: The response says Gomez has become less convinced that scaling alone is sufficient, but does not say observed gains led him to provisionally believe scaling could deliver all needed capabilities.

r002.rationale: He says he is less convinced scaling alone gets everything needed and that adding compute to the current recipe will not produce every capability sought.

sol-6.1.text:
I’ve become less convinced that scaling alone will get us everything we need. For a while, it was tempting to think you could just keep making the model bigger, feed it more data, and all the missing capabilities would emerge. And scaling has been extraordinarily productive, so you shouldn’t dismiss it. But I think that picture is incomplete.

The distinction is between a model that can produce a plausible answer and a system that can reliably accomplish a task. For the latter, you need more than knowledge compressed into weights. You need the ability to interact with an environment, get feedback, correct mistakes, and keep working toward an objective. A larger model can help with all of that, but it doesn’t automatically give you the right learning process.

So I still expect substantial gains from scale. I just think more of the progress will come from changing how we train these systems and how we let them act, rather than assuming that the next increase in parameter count will solve every remaining problem.

r001.rationale: The response says it was tempting to think scaling would produce all missing capabilities and that scaling has been productive, but does not clearly state that Aidan himself provisionally believed this because of observed capability gains.

r002.rationale: He says he has become less convinced scaling alone will provide everything needed and that the next increase in model size will not solve every remaining problem.
